label: Internment of warships
description: A neutral port could offer a warship refuge, but could not let it serve indefinitely as a wartime base. An interned ship was detained, and its crew prevented from returning to combat. For the squadron, that meant losing the ship for the rest of the war, even if she remained intact.

sources.title: A. V. Kudashkin. Internment — Great Russian Encyclopedia

label: Roadstead: an anchorage
description: A roadstead is an area of water where ships lie at anchor. An inner roadstead lies within the sheltered waters of a port; an outer roadstead is on its approaches. Lying in the outer roadstead and sheltering inside the harbour therefore expose ships to different conditions, even at the same base.

sources.title: V. A. Dygalo. The Russian Fleet: Selected Naval Terms

label: Counting ships by pennants
description: A pennant is a long, narrow naval flag. In a phrase such as “a squadron of 66 pennants”, however, it stands for a ship: one pennant means one vessel. The total alone tells us little about the squadron’s composition or strength—a battleship and a small torpedo boat each count as one.

label: Shrapnel
description: A shrapnel shell was filled with bullets. A time fuze allowed it to burst in the air, releasing the bullets against people in the open. In a memoir, “coming under shrapnel” therefore means coming under artillery fire particularly dangerous to anyone who had not reached cover.

sources.title: Shrapnel — Great Soviet Encyclopedia, first edition, vol. LXII, col. 654

label: Parapet
description: An earth bank in front of a trench, protecting soldiers from enemy fire and observation. They could fire over it, using its edge to support their weapons. Anyone who climbed onto the parapet and stood upright was stepping out from behind that protection.

label: Casemate in a fort
description: A protected room inside a fortification. Casemates housed troops, stores, guns or riflemen; their walls and roofs were intended to withstand enemy fire. In an account of a fort’s defence, the word means this kind of shelter, rather than a prison cell—another meaning of the Russian word.

sources.title: Casemates — Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopedic Dictionary, vol. XIIIa, pp. 924–925

label: Fanza: a Chinese village house
description: Russian accounts of China used fanza for a village house. Its walls were often built with clay, and its roof thatched with straw or reeds. Inside, a broad sleeping platform might be warmed by a flue running beneath it from the stove. The word refers to homes, rather than military buildings.

sources.title: Fanza — Great Soviet Encyclopedia, first edition, vol. LVI, col. 609

label: Concession
description: A state granted a private operator the right, on agreed terms, to exploit natural resources or build and run an economic undertaking. A contract set out that right for a specified period. Here the concessions concern timber and a railway; obtaining one did not mean acquiring ownership of the territory itself.

sources.title: Ye. E. Chukovskaya. Concession — Great Russian Encyclopedia

label: War indemnity
description: A payment demanded by the victor from a defeated state after a war. Peace negotiations concerned not only borders and ports, but also whether such a payment would be made and how much it would be. In another sense, the Russian word also meant compulsory levies on people in occupied territory.

label: Halftone printing
description: A way of preparing photographs for print: smooth transitions of light and shade are converted into many tiny dots, from which a printing plate is made. On paper, the dots together give the impression of continuous tones, allowing photographs to be reproduced in an ordinary print run.
